claim: Hair cells are specialized sensors located in the inner ear that enable the transduction of sound, motion, and gravity into neuronal impulses.
source: Hair cells are specialized sensors located in the inner ear that enable the transduction of sound, motion, and gravity into neuronal impulses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Torres and Giráldez, 1998, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In birds some hair cells contain an iron-rich organelle, the cuticulosome, that has been implicated in the magnetic sense.
source: In birds some hair cells contain an iron-rich organelle, the cuticulosome, that has been implicated in the magnetic sense.
evidence: This is a statement of established findings from prior research, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: The cuticulosome forms rapidly after hatching in a process that involves vesicle fusion and nucleation of ferritin nanoparticles.
source: We show that this organelle forms rapidly after hatching in a process that involves vesicle fusion and nucleation of ferritin nanoparticles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from histological, transcriptomic, and tomographic methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Transcripts involved in endocytosis, extracellular exosomes, and metal ion binding are differentially expressed in cuticulosome positive hair cells.
source: We further report that transcripts involved in endocytosis, extracellular exosomes, and metal ion binding are differentially expressed in cuticulosome positive hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cuticulosome and the associated molecular machinery regulate the concentration of iron within the labyrinth of the inner ear.
source: These data suggest that the cuticulosome and the associated molecular machinery regulate the concentration of iron within the labyrinth of the inner ear, which might indirectly tune a magnetic sensor that relies on electromagnetic induction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Mechanical deflection of stereocilia opens cation channels via filamentous structures called tip-links, resulting in cation influx and neurotransmitter release.
source: Displacement of stereocilia opens cation channels via filamentous structures called tip-links, resulting in cation influx, and subsequently neurotransmitter release (Pickles et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pickles et al., 1984, representing established knowledge.

claim: Stereocilia are composed of tightly packed parallel filaments of f-actin, which taper at their base forming a rootlet that inserts into the cuticular plate.
source: Stereocilia are composed of tightly packed parallel filaments of f-actin, which taper at their base forming a rootlet that inserts into the cuticular plate (Pollock and McDermott, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pollock and McDermott, 2015, representing established knowledge.

claim: The cuticular plate is a meshwork of actin at the base of the stereocilia that has a characteristic U-shape and is believed to provide stability to the hair bundle.
source: The latter is a meshwork of actin at the base of the stereocilia that has a characteristic U-shape and is believed to provide stability to the hair bundle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell structure.

claim: The kinocillium inserts into the cuticular plate serving as an important guidepost for stereocilia development and orientation.
source: The kinocillium, with its distinctive core of microtubules, also inserts into the cuticular plate serving as an important guidepost for stereocilia development and orientation (Montcouquiol et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Montcouquiol et al., 2003, representing established knowledge.

claim: Neurons within the vestibular nuclei of pigeons are responsive to weak magnetic stimuli.
source: Following the studies of Dickman and colleagues, who reported that neurons within the vestibular nuclei of pigeons are responsive to weak magnetic stimuli, we conducted a histological analysis of the inner ear of birds employing the Prussian blue stain which labels ferric iron (Wu and Dickman, 2011, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wu and Dickman, 2011, 2012.

claim: Cuticulosomes are approximately 400–500 nm in diameter.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that cuticulosomes are approximately 400–500 nm in diameter and 25% are encapsulated by a visible membrane.
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy measurements reported in prior work (Lauwers et al., 2013).

claim: 25% of cuticulosomes are encapsulated by a visible membrane.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that cuticulosomes are approximately 400–500 nm in diameter and 25% are encapsulated by a visible membrane.
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy observations reported in prior work.

claim: Each cuticulosome consists of tens of thousands of ferritin-like granules.
source: Each cuticulosome consists of tens of thousands of ferritin-like granules, which have a distinct paracrystalline organization in some but not all cases.
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy observations.

claim: Cuticulosomes can be found in all sensory epithelia of the inner ear.
source: Cuticulosomes can be found in all sensory epithelia of the inner ear, however, they are most prevalent in the avian equivalent of the organ of Corti.
evidence: This is based on histological observations from prior work.

claim: Approximately 30% of hair cells in the basilar papilla are cuticulosome positive.
source: In this structure, known as the basilar papilla, approximately 30% of hair cells are cuticulosome positive.
evidence: This is based on quantitative histological analysis from prior work.

claim: Cuticulosomes are an evolutionary conserved feature in a broad range of avian species.
source: A phylogenic analysis of adult birds revealed that cuticulosomes are an evolutionary conserved feature in a broad range of avian species (e.g. zebra finches, ducks, chickens and ostriches) but are absent in mice, humans and fish.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis from prior work.

claim: Cuticulosomes are absent in mice, humans and fish.
source: A phylogenic analysis of adult birds revealed that cuticulosomes are an evolutionary conserved feature in a broad range of avian species (e.g. zebra finches, ducks, chickens and ostriches) but are absent in mice, humans and fish.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis from prior work.

claim: In 1 day old birds only 2.46 ± 0.95% of hair cells in the basilar papilla were cuticulosome positive.
source: In 1 day old birds only a small percentage of hair cells in the basilar papilla were cuticulosome positive (2.46 ± 0.95%, n = 4 birds), whereas they were plentiful at 8 days (23.66 ± 3.03%, n = 3 birds), 16 days (31.19 ± 2.86%, n = 6 birds), 30 days (36.9 ± 3.56%, n = 5 birds), and 1 year of age (24.92 ± 6.74%, n = 3 birds) (Figure 1c and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative histological data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: At day 1 and day 8 the distribution of PB positive hair cells appears stochastic.
source: At day 1 and day 8 the distribution of PB positive hair cells appears stochastic, however, at subsequent time points we observed a noticeable enrichment of cuticulosomes in the distal regions of the basilar papilla (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–6).
evidence: This is based on spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 1 supplements 2-6.

claim: At subsequent time points after day 8, there is a noticeable enrichment of cuticulosomes in the distal regions of the basilar papilla.
source: At day 1 and day 8 the distribution of PB positive hair cells appears stochastic, however, at subsequent time points we observed a noticeable enrichment of cuticulosomes in the distal regions of the basilar papilla (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–6).
evidence: This is based on spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 1 supplements 2-6.

claim: Almost all cuticulosomes were located opposite the stereocilia.
source: Strikingly, almost all cuticulosomes were located opposite the stereocillia.
evidence: This is based on whole mount Prussian blue staining observations.

claim: The position of the cuticulosome gradually changes with time, from a lateral localization close to the border of the cell in 1 day old birds, to a more medial localization closer to the stereocilia in 1 year old birds.
source: This revealed that the position of the cuticulosome gradually changes with time, from a lateral localization, close to the border of the cell in 1 day old birds, to a more medial localization closer to the stereocilia, in 1 year old birds (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: In 1 day old birds the cuticulosome is closest to the apical cell surface, and it gradually adopts a deeper position within the cuticular plate over the course of a year.
source: We observed that in 1 day old birds the cuticulosome is closest to the apical cell surface, and that it gradually adopts a deeper position within the cuticular plate over the course of a year (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: At 1 day of age, 100% of cuticulosomes were in the process of formation.
source: At 1 day of age we observed that 100% of organelles were in the process of formation (n = 3 birds, n = 4 cuticulosomes), which gradually decreased to 34.6% at 8 days (n = 3 birds, n = 26 cuticulosomes), 22.2% at 16 days (n = 3 birds, n = 45 cuticulosomes) and 17.6% at 30 days (n = 3 birds, n = 17 cuticulosomes) (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on transmission electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only 7% of organelles in 1 year old pigeon hair cells appeared to be incomplete.
source: In contrast, only 7% of organelles in 1 year old pigeon hair cells appeared to be incomplete (Lauwers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on data from a prior publication (Lauwers et al., 2013).

claim: In 1 day old birds, there was no evidence of paracrystalline ordering of ferritin-like granules.
source: In 1 day old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 4 cuticulosomes), we did not observe any evidence of paracrystalline ordering in contrast to 16 day old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 26 cuticulosomes) where ordering of granules was observed in 17.8% of cases (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy observations.

claim: In 16 day old birds, ordering of granules was observed in 17.8% of cases.
source: In 1 day old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 4 cuticulosomes), we did not observe any evidence of paracrystalline ordering in contrast to 16 day old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 26 cuticulosomes) where ordering of granules was observed in 17.8% of cases (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy observations.

claim: Cuticulosome size increased from 296.4 nm ± 69.2 nm in 1 day old birds to 387.9 ± 29 nm in 8 day old birds.
source: This maturation coincided with an increase in cuticulosome size from 296.4 nm ± 69.2 nm in 1 day old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 4 cuticulosomes), to 387.9 ± 29 nm in 8 day old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 26 cuticulosomes), 580.7 nm ± 21.7 nm in 16 days old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 45 cuticulosomes), and 514.3 ± 38 nm in 30 day old birds (n = 3 birds, n = 17 cuticulosomes) (Figure 2k).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements from electron microscopy shown in Figure 2k.

claim: The percentage of cuticulosomes surrounded by lipid membranes was similar at 1 day, 8 days, 16 days, 30 days and 1 year.
source: The percentage of cuticulosomes surrounded by lipid membranes was similar at 1 day, 8 days, 16 days, 30 days and 1 year (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy observations.

claim: At 1 day of age, 100% of cuticulosomes were associated with vesicles.
source: We found that at 1 day of age 100% of cuticulosomes were associated with vesicles (n = 3 birds, n = 4 cuticulosomes), 46.15% at 8 days (n = 3 birds, n = 26 cuticulosomes), 24.44% at 16 days (n = 3 birds, n = 45 cuticulosomes), 52.94% at 30 days (n = 3 birds, n = 17 cuticulosomes) and 25% at 1 year (Lauwers et al., 2013) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy observations.

claim: At 8 days post hatching, cuticulosomes are decorated by numerous vesicles that range in size from 30 nm to 200 nm.
source: This suggests that at 8 days post hatching cuticulosomes are decorated by numerous vesicles that range in size from 30 nm to 200 nm (Figure 3a–l).
evidence: This is based on electron tomography data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Some vesicles contain ferritin-like nanoparticles and appear to be fusing with the larger organelle.
source: Some, but not all, of these vesicles contain ferritin-like nanoparticles and appear to be fusing with the larger organelle (Figure 3e–f,h–i).
evidence: This is based on electron tomography observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Vesicles traffic from the periphery of the cuticular plate to the cuticulosome.
source: We again observed the trafficking of vesicles from the periphery of the cuticular plate to the cuticulosome and in rare instances invaginations of the apical membrane indicative of an endocytotic/exocytotic event (Figure 3k–l).
evidence: This is based on electron tomography observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: There are no actin free tunnels within the cuticular plate that would serve as subcellular conduits to the cuticulosome.
source: We did not observe any actin free tunnels within the cuticular plate, which would serve as subcellular conduits to the cuticulosome.
evidence: This is based on electron tomography observations.

claim: The actin-rich meshwork that surrounds the cuticulosome is largely uniform, with the exception of vesicles.
source: This revealed, that with the exception of vesicles, the actin-rich meshwork that surrounds the cuticulosome is largely uniform (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on quantitative staining intensity analysis shown in Figure 2 supplement 1.

claim: The cuticulosome contains heavy chain ferritin.
source: This experiment revealed the presence of heavy chain ferritin throughout the cytoplasm of hair cells, with a notable punctate structure that coincided with the location of the cuticulosome in pigeons aged 1 day (n = 3 birds), 8 day (n = 2 birds) and 1 year (n = 3 birds) (Figure 4d–i).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 4.

claim: The expression of heavy chain ferritin peaks at 16 days of age.
source: This experiment revealed that the expression of heavy chain ferritin peaks at 16 days of age, but is consistently high at all developmental time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4 supplement 1.

claim: Heavy chain ferritin is consistently expressed at high levels throughout development.
source: This experiment revealed that the expression of heavy chain ferritin peaks at 16 days of age, but is consistently high at all developmental time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4 supplement 1.

claim: The dominant iron species in ferritin is the iron-oxide ferrihydrite.
source: It is well established that the dominant iron species in ferritin is the iron-oxide ferrihydrite, but it has also been reported to contain phases of magnetite (Fe2+Fe3+2O4) and maghemite (Fe2O3) (Cowley et al., 2000; Quintana et al., 2004; Gossuin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cowley et al., 2000; Quintana et al., 2004; Gossuin et al., 2005, representing established knowledge.

claim: Ferritin has been reported to contain phases of magnetite and maghemite.
source: It is well established that the dominant iron species in ferritin is the iron-oxide ferrihydrite, but it has also been reported to contain phases of magnetite (Fe2+Fe3+2O4) and maghemite (Fe2O3) (Cowley et al., 2000; Quintana et al., 2004; Gossuin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cowley et al., 2000; Quintana et al., 2004; Gossuin et al., 2005.

claim: There is a sharp increase in Turnbull blue staining in the basilar papilla and lagena from hatching to 30 days.
source: We observed a sharp increase in Turnbull blue staining in the basilar papilla and lagena from hatching to 30 days, mirroring the results of our Prussian Blue staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on Turnbull Blue staining data shown in Figure 4 supplement 2.

claim: The cuticulosome contains Fe2+ at low levels.
source: These data indicate that the cuticulosome is composed of ferritin and that it contains Fe2+ at low levels, consistent with the presence of multiple iron oxide species.
evidence: This is inferred from Turnbull Blue staining results.

claim: 11,300 transcripts with mean FPKM > 1 were identified in the transcriptomic analysis.
source: In total we identified 11,300 transcripts (mean FPKM > 1) with 10,277 (90.1%) having an annotated function (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data.

claim: The development of the cuticular plate begins at embryonic day 8 in chickens.
source: The development of the cuticular plate, which is closely associated with the formation of stereocilia, begins at embryonic day 8 in chickens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chicken hair cell development.

claim: At embryonic day 8 in chickens, the cuticular plate is primarily occupied by vesicles, mitochondria, and lysosomes.
source: At this time it is primarily occupied by vesicles, mitochondria, and lysosomes, before growing basally until embryonic day 14 when it resembles that present in the adult cochlea (Tilney and DeRosier, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tilney and DeRosier, 1986.

claim: Post hatching, the cuticular plate is so dense that it excludes all organelles, even ribosomes.
source: Post hatching the cuticular plate, with its web of actin filaments, is considered to be so dense that it excludes all organelles, even ribosomes (Corwin and Warchol, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Corwin and Warchol, 1991.

claim: Hair cells have a specialized zone close to the cell border that serves as a highway for subcellular structures that support membrane recycling.
source: To enable the passage of vesicles to and from the apical membrane hair cells have a specialized zone close to the cell border that serves as a highway for subcellular structures that support membrane recycling (Kachar et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kachar et al., 1997.

claim: The formation of the cuticulosome is initiated at the apical cellular border opposite the kinocilium.
source: Our data indicate that the formation of the cuticulosome is initiated at the apical cellular border opposite the kinocilium.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental and spatial data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cuticulosome is formed by the fusion of vesicles, some containing ferritin.
source: It appears that the cuticulosome is formed by the fusion of vesicles, some containing ferritin, that result in an organelle that increases in size and density (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from electron microscopy and tomography data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Vesicles are transported into the cuticular plate from the lateral boundary.
source: It appears that these vesicles are transported into the cuticular plate from the lateral boundary.
evidence: This is inferred from electron tomography observations.

claim: Cell lines that overexpress either wildtype Rab5 or a constitutively active form (rab5:Q79L) develop enlarged early endosomes.
source: Notably, cell lines that overexpress either wildtype Rab5 or a constitutiveIy active form (rab5:Q79L) develop enlarged early endosomes (Roberts et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 1999.

claim: The reduced expression levels of RNF128 and increased expression of RAB5B in cuticulosome positive cells may license the formation of a large membrane bound organelle within the cell.
source: It is therefore conceivable that the reduced expression levels of RNF128 and increased expression of RAB5B we observe in cuticulosome positive cells, licenses the formation of such a large membrane bound organelle within the cell.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the transcriptomic data and known functions of these genes.

claim: Pigeons begin to fly at approximately one month of age.
source: This is a tempting proposition given that pigeons begin to fly at approximately one month of age, a time when the cuticulosome is on the cusp of maturation (Hazard, 1922; Nam and Lee, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hazard, 1922; Nam and Lee, 2006.

claim: Chickens aged 10 days can be conditioned to a magnetic anomaly.
source: Wiltschko and colleagues have reported that chickens aged 10 days can be conditioned to a magnetic anomaly (Denzau et al., 2011) and juvenile European Robins are known to possess a magnetic sense (Muheim et al., 2002), whereas pigeons aged 12 weeks are disorientated if they are transported in the dark (Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Denzau et al., 2011.

claim: Juvenile European Robins possess a magnetic sense.
source: Wiltschko and colleagues have reported that chickens aged 10 days can be conditioned to a magnetic anomaly (Denzau et al., 2011) and juvenile European Robins are known to possess a magnetic sense (Muheim et al., 2002), whereas pigeons aged 12 weeks are disorientated if they are transported in the dark (Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muheim et al., 2002.

claim: Pigeons aged 12 weeks are disoriented if they are transported in the dark.
source: Wiltschko and colleagues have reported that chickens aged 10 days can be conditioned to a magnetic anomaly (Denzau et al., 2011) and juvenile European Robins are known to possess a magnetic sense (Muheim et al., 2002), whereas pigeons aged 12 weeks are disorientated if they are transported in the dark (Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1981.

claim: The formation of the cuticulosome is not the product of late-onset iron accumulation.
source: The data presented in this manuscript strongly suggest that the formation of the cuticulosome is not the product of late-onset iron accumulation, and is more likely the result of a genetically encoded developmental or homeostatic program.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental timing and molecular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The formation of the cuticulosome is more likely the result of a genetically encoded developmental or homeostatic program.
source: The data presented in this manuscript strongly suggest that the formation of the cuticulosome is not the product of late-onset iron accumulation, and is more likely the result of a genetically encoded developmental or homeostatic program.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental timing and molecular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Based on current understanding of the magnetic properties of ferritin, the cuticulosome lacks sufficient magnetic susceptibility in an Earth strength magnetic field to open a mechanosensitive channel.
source: Firstly, based on our current understanding of the magnetic properties of ferritin, the cuticulosome lacks sufficient magnetic susceptibility in an Earth strength magnetic field to open a mechanosensitive channel, and, secondly, there seems to be no direct physical connection with the apical membrane that would mediate the transfer of a force (Jandacka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on inference from known properties of ferritin and citation to Jandacka et al., 2015.

claim: There is no direct physical connection between the cuticulosome and the apical membrane that would mediate the transfer of a force.
source: Firstly, based on our current understanding of the magnetic properties of ferritin, the cuticulosome lacks sufficient magnetic susceptibility in an Earth strength magnetic field to open a mechanosensitive channel, and, secondly, there seems to be no direct physical connection with the apical membrane that would mediate the transfer of a force (Jandacka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on structural observations and citation to Jandacka et al., 2015.

claim: The cuticulosome appears to move deeper into the cuticular plate away from the apical membrane as it matures.
source: Indeed the cuticulosome appears to move deeper into the cuticular plate away from the apical membrane as it matures.
evidence: This is based on developmental positional data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The cuticulosome might play an indirect role in the magnetic sense by influencing the ionic concentration of the endolymph.
source: A third possibility is that the cuticulosome plays an indirect role in the magnetic sense by influencing the ionic concentration of the endolymph.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The detection of magnetic fields may rely on electromagnetic induction within the semicircular canals with the endolymph serving as a conductor.
source: A number of investigators have proposed that the detection of magnetic fields may rely on electromagnetic induction within the semicircular canals - the endolymph serving as a conductor (Viguier, 1882; Jungerman and Rosenblum, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Viguier, 1882; Jungerman and Rosenblum, 1980.

claim: The cuticulosome, coupled with the vesicular machinery associated with it, might regulate the conductivity of the endolymph by adjusting the concentration of cations.
source: The cuticulosome, coupled with the vesicular machinery associated with it, might represent a means of regulating the conductivity of the endolymph by adjusting the concentration of cations, thereby tuning a magnetic sensor reliant on electromagnetic induction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The cuticulosome may serve as a precursor for a magnetite-based magnetoreceptor located elsewhere in the inner ear.
source: Alternatively, the cuticulosome may serve as a precursor for a magnetite-based magnetoreceptor located elsewhere in the inner ear.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.
